title: Person Gesturing No Emoji 🙅 Meaning: The Crossed-Arm X
description: The person gesturing no emoji 🙅 crosses both arms into an X: “no,” “not allowed,” or “absolutely not.” The gesture comes from Japan. See how it compares with 🚫.
summary: 🙅 shows a person crossing their forearms in an X in front of their body. It means no: refusal, disapproval, “not allowed,” or “don’t even think about it.” The gesture comes from Japan, where crossed arms signal that something is wrong or forbidden, and online it delivers a firm but often playful rejection.
meaning: In Japan, forming an X with your arms is an everyday way to say no, wrong or not permitted. The mark is called batsu, the counterpart to the circle, maru, that means yes or correct. Emoji originated on Japanese phones, so the gesture came along, paired with 🙆, the person making an O overhead for “OK.” Unicode’s original name for 🙅 was “Face With No Good Gesture.”

English speakers adopted it as an emphatic, slightly theatrical no. It is stronger than a thumbs down and more human than a 🚫 sign. People use it to turn down plans (“camping in January? 🙅”), to reject ideas, foods, exes and trends, and to set limits: “no work talk tonight 🙅.” It usually carries personality, like someone physically blocking the suggestion.

Boundaries are a major theme. The emoji shows up in posts about refusing toxic behavior, quitting bad habits and protecting one’s time, where it works as a visual “not today.” The woman variant, 🙅‍♀️, is particularly common in this self-assured register and in memes about saying no to drama. It turns a refusal into a stance, which is why it pairs so naturally with talk of self-respect.

Its meaning can also be plainly informational. Event organizers, teachers and community moderators use 🙅 to flag what is not allowed, such as “🙅 no outside food.” Because the pose is unfamiliar as a real-life gesture in many Western countries, a few people misread it as crossing arms in self-defense or a dance move, but the surrounding “no” nearly always clarifies it.

contexts.label: In texting
contexts.body: It is a quick, expressive refusal: “are you coming out tonight?” “🙅 I’m in pajamas.” Friends use it to veto restaurants, movie picks and bad dating decisions. The tone is generally light, since a truly angry no tends to come in words. Doubling or tripling it adds comic insistence. It is refusal as performance, meant to get a laugh.

contexts.label: On TikTok and Instagram
contexts.body: Captions use it for lists of things the creator will not tolerate or products they do not recommend, often alongside ❌. It appears in “green flags and red flags” content and in self-care posts about boundaries. In comments, 🙅 voices disagreement with a take without starting a long argument. The human figure makes the rejection feel like a personal stance.

contexts.label: Around the world
contexts.body: The crossed-arm X is instantly understood in Japan and widely recognized in South Korea and other parts of East Asia as “no” or “incorrect.” Elsewhere people know it mainly through emoji and game shows. Its partner 🙆, arms in a circle, means OK in the same system, though outside Asia it is often misread.

contexts.label: At work
contexts.body: It suits informal rules and reminders, such as “🙅 no meetings on Friday afternoons,” and good-humored pushback among peers. As a response to a colleague’s proposal it can feel like a blunt shutdown, so pair it with a reason. With clients or senior leaders, a written “unfortunately we can’t” is safer.

combos.meaning: No and yes, or wrong and right, as a pair of options.
Rejecting a red flag or deal-breaker.
Stop right there; not having it.

confusedWith.difference: 🙆 raises both arms into a circle above the head, the Japanese gesture for OK or correct. 🙅 crosses the arms into an X for no or incorrect. They are opposites.
🚫 is an impersonal sign for rules and bans. 🙅 is a person refusing, so it conveys attitude and is better for personal boundaries and opinions.
❌ marks something as wrong, cancelled or deleted, as in a checklist. 🙅 says the same no with a human face and body language attached.

avoid: Do not use it to reject someone’s heartfelt request or invitation without any words, which feels cold.
Avoid it as a lone reply to a colleague’s idea in a shared channel.
Skip it in serious refusals involving safety or consent, where plain language is essential.
design: The person is shown from the chest up with forearms crossed in an X in front of the chest or face, typically with a stern or neutral expression. Platforms differ in clothing color and how high the arms are held. It comes in a gender-neutral form plus woman 🙅‍♀️ and man 🙅‍♂️ versions, all with skin tone support.

faqs.q: What does 🙅‍♀️ mean from a girl?
faqs.a: She is saying no, and usually with some sass. It may be a refusal of plans, a rejection of an idea, or a statement that she will not put up with something. Among friends it is playful. In response to a romantic advance, take it as a clear no.

faqs.q: What does 🙅‍♂️ mean from a guy?
faqs.a: It means “no,” “no way,” or “not happening.” He might be turning down an invitation, disagreeing with you, or joking about something he refuses to do. The tone is usually lighthearted unless the conversation is serious.

faqs.q: Why does the 🙅 emoji cross its arms?
faqs.a: The pose reproduces a Japanese gesture. Crossing the arms or index fingers into an X, called batsu, signals no, wrong or not allowed in Japan. Emoji were first developed there, so this culturally specific sign became part of the global set.

The intended opposite is 🙆, a person forming a circle with their arms overhead to mean OK or correct. In casual use, people also treat 👍, ✅ and 🙋 as affirmative counterparts, since the arms-overhead gesture is less familiar outside East Asia.
